He welcomed Washington’s approach to talks with Russia, saying coordinated international action must create the conditions for Moscow to end its aggression against Ukraine. by Kyiv Post | Aug. 28, 2026, 8:48 pm Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied CIA Director John Ratcliffe testifies during a Senate Committee on Intelligence hearing on worldwide threats, March 18, 2026. (Photo by Oliver Contreras / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip Ukraine received information from the US regarding several meetings CIA Director John Ratcliffe held with Russian intelligence officials, following his unannounced trip to Moscow on Tuesday, Aug. 25. President Volodymyr Zelensky said Friday, Aug. 28, that Kyiv had discussed the developments with US officials before and after the Moscow meetings. He also thanked the American side for sharing information and for what he called the necessary tone in its diplomatic contacts with Russia. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . “We value the coordination of steps and the fact that America is advancing a thoroughly realistic vision of what needs to be done and what must be done,” Zelensky said. “Russia must end its war; all conditions must be created to make that happen,” he continued. Advertisement Ratcliffe’s secretive visit CBS News reported the visit on Tuesday, citing sources familiar with the matter after a US Air Force Boeing C-17 Globemaster III military transport plane landed at Moscow’s Vnukovo Airport . The plane flew in from Riga, Latvia, raising questions about the flight’s unusual route. The US aircraft – identified as RCH4555 – departed Riga at around 8:50 a.m. before landing at Vnukovo Airport at roughly 10:04 a.m. Flight-tracking data indicated that the aircraft first arrived in Riga on Sunday, Aug. 23, after departing from Camp Springs, Maryland, home to Andrews Air Force Base . Neither Moscow nor Washington commented on the purpose of the visit, or publicly identified the US official that arrived in Russia at the time. Other Topics of Interest Italy’s Crosetto Appoints Fedorov as Defense Innovation Adviser Mykhailo Fedorov said he will help Italy develop modern warfare technologies while continuing work on Ukrainian defense projects. “We have no information about this,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said when asked about the aircraft, adding that Russia was not planning meetings with the US administration. Reports of possible attack on NATO Several media outlets, including Axios and Suspilne , reported that Washington had informed Kyiv, ahead of the reported visit, that a high-level US delegation was traveling to Moscow and had asked Ukraine to refrain from strikes on both Moscow and St. Petersburg. Advertisement On Wednesday, Aug. 26, The Wall Street Journal and Politico reported that Ratcliffe made the visit to warn Russian President Vladimir Putin against attacking a NATO member. Around the same time, US President Donald Trump said that “something may come out of” the visit, adding that his administration was working “very hard to end the war in Ukraine,” despite initially downplaying Ratcliffe’s visit as routine. Russia weighs escalation Meanwhile, Bloomberg reported that Russia is considering intensifying ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine, after concluding that peace negotiations have “reached a dead end.” According to the sources, all attempts at negotiations have effectively collapsed, leaving Ukraine and Russia back at square one. Bloomberg , citing anonymous sources close to the Kremlin, said Moscow increasingly sees Ukrainian strikes as attacks by NATO, because alliance members supply Kyiv with weapons and intelligence. On Thursday, Aug. 27, Trump dismissed the possibility of Russia attacking NATO while rejecting reports that Ratcliffe traveled to Moscow to warn the Kremlin against such a move. “There was no message and there was nothing unusual,” he continued. “I am not concerned… at all. There is no problem.” Advertisement Russia confirms visit According to Axios , Sergey Naryshkin, director of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR), confirmed on Thursday that he met Ratcliffe during his trip to Moscow. He described their discussions as a regular part of intelligence work and said there was “nothing out of the ordinary.” So far, Moscow continues to dismiss the prospect of a ceasefire and has yet to join the negotiating table, which Ukraine is seeking to encourage by targeting Russia’s critical oil and energy infrastructure , alongside the logistics network. According to The New York Times on Thursday, Ratcliffe warned Russian intelligence officials that Moscow’s military and economic position would deteriorate further if the Kremlin refused to pursue serious peace negotiations. Ratcliffe delivered the warning directly to Aleksandr Bortnikov , head of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB), according to current and former US officials cited by NYT. Photograph: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/Shutterstock OpenAI OpenAI disclose another hack on government department in Australia Attack accessing historical data on bushfires occurred in June but not disclosed by the tech company until Thursday Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Henry Belot Fri 2 Oct 2026 06.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Artificial intelligence company OpenAI has disclosed another unauthorised hack on a government department in Australia. In June, an OpenAI agent hacked into a New South Wales state government department and accessed historical non-public data on bushfires without authorisation. The breach, which comes weeks after news of a similar hack on a federal government department involving Medicare data , was not reported by the US based company until Thursday. The NSW Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water is now working with the state’s cyber security agency to investigate the breach. The Australian Signals Directorate has also been informed of the hack on the NSW national parks and wildlife service. OpenAI told the NSW government that its agent had operated beyond its intended use and the statistics it obtained were not publicly available. The company first became aware of the breach on Tuesday and conducted a 48 hours review to determine its scope before informing the NSW premier’s office. “The results we reviewed do not show that the model retrieved any personal information,” an OpenAI spokesperson said. This latest breach has added to calls for tougher regulation of AI companies and for bolstered cyber security defences. “We simply cannot trust these companies. They have no respect for the sovereignty of our governments, of our way of life,” Greens MP Abigail Boyd said. Boyd said it was damning that the breach occurred in June but the government was not notified until this week. “We clearly cannot rely on these multinational big tech companies to comply with even the most minimal of social obligations such as notifying when, or even taking enough care to notice if, their products are hacking government systems,” Boyd said. On Wednesday, the department of home affairs on Wednesday told federal departments to examine their older software and ensure cyber security was up to date. The prime minister expressed his “extreme concern” about at an OpenAI agent hacking Australian Institute of Health and Welfare in June. The Victorian Department of Health and the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research were also compromised by an OpenAI agent. An artificial intelligence agent is a system that autonomously solves problems, makes decisions, plans and performs complex tasks on behalf of another user or system, using all available tools. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv claims half of Russia’s oil refining capacity destroyed Ukraine says its long-range strikes have hurt Russian economy while Vladimir Putin concedes they have cost Russia roughly 1% of GDP. What we know on day 1,686 Guardian staff and agencies Mon 5 Oct 2026 21.27 EDT Last modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 23.19 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Long-range Ukrainian strikes have taken out more than half of Russia’s oil refining capacity, hampering Moscow’s ability to supply its forces during the war, the defence ministry in Kyiv has claimed. Ukrainian forces have repeatedly attacked refineries from Moscow to Siberia, sparking a widespread fuel crisis in Russia earlier this year that forced authorities to restrict petrol sales. “Fifty-one per cent of struck refining capacity is a significant blow to the enemy’s economy, to its ability to carry out aggression and supply its troop groupings,” Ukrainian defence minister Yevhenii Khmara said. “Our deep strikes continue to bring the war to Russian territory.” Russian officials have not released figures on damage to the country’s oil infrastructure. But in a rare acknowledgment of the strikes’ economic impact , Vladimir Putin said they had cost Russia roughly 1% of its gross domestic product. “They started attacking oil refineries and openly declared the goal of damaging our economy. Did they achieve their goal? Partially,” the Russian president told a meeting of the Valdai Club forum of international foreign policy experts last Thursday. Donald Trump has blamed Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries for high petrol prices, saying the Iran war was no longer responsible. “What’s driving up Gasoline is no longer the strait of Hormuz, because Record Numbers of Barrels are coming out now on an almost daily basis, but the word, ‘Refineries,’ where Russia’s are being blown up by Ukraine,” the US president posted on his Truth Social platform. Six people were killed and nearly 60 injured when Russian bombs struck a residential area of Ukraine’s north-eastern city of Kharkiv on Monday, officials said. Rescue workers led stunned ‌residents out of badly damaged buildings and flats, guiding them carefully around piles of rubble. Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-largest city, lies close to the Russian border and has come under regular shelling and drone attacks since Moscow invaded in February 2022. French president Emmanuel Macron condemned Russia’s decision to scale up strikes on civilian infrastructure , saying Moscow “has made the irresponsible choice to intensify its strikes on civilian infrastructure and targets”. View image in fullscreen Rescuers work at the site of a sewing factory damaged by a Russian airstrike in Kharkiv on Monday. Photograph: Sofiia Gatilova/Reuters Russian drones struck a grain ship in the Black Sea on Monday, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, after Romania reported a ship had caught fire and sunk near its coast with two crew members killed. “A horrific strike by two Russian drones on a civilian vessel in neutral waters carrying corn,” the Ukrainian president said on X, adding that the ship was Turkish-owned and that Azerbaijani and Indian nationals were onboard. Romanian authorities said two crew members had died and 11 were rescued after the 139-metre-long (455 foot) Royad Mammadov caught fire in the Black Sea, an increasing battlefield for drone attacks in the war. War-related objects found in the Black Sea had more than doubled in six months, maritime risk expert Ambrey said last month in a report. At least a third of them carried live payloads. The objects include unexploded ordnance, drones and other unmanned vehicles found washed ashore or floating at sea, it said. Ukrainian drones attacked two facilities at the Russian-held ⁠Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant in south-eastern Ukraine overnight on Monday, but there was no threat to nuclear safety, the ⁠head of Russia’s state ⁠nuclear corporation ​said . Alexei Likhachev, director general of Rosatom, said a driver delivering food for plant employees was killed in the drone attack. According ⁠to Likhachev, a laboratory building and a radioactive waste processing plant were the targets. Ukraine has not commented on the incident. Ukraine has begun using artificial intelligence-enabled robot guns to take down Russia’s new and fast-moving jet-powered drones. For months, Kyiv has been seeking a way to intercept the new Russian drones pounding the Ukrainian capital, even as it faces a dire lack of suitable ammunition to take them out. Presidential adviser Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov said on social media that 12 automated turrets had been installed in Kyiv to counter jet-powered Shahed drones, with more planned. Ukraine’s air force later said it had used the robotic turrets to successfully shoot down Russian jet-powered drones, including the Geran-5, for the first time. “It’s machine vision that is used for the shootdowns,” air force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said on Ukrainian television. “Artificial intelligence makes it possible to engage even jet-powered drones.” Germany’s foreign intelligence chief has warned that the country risks being drawn into a conflict with Russia as hybrid attacks ordered by Moscow increase. Martin Jaeger, head of Germany’s BND spy service, told lawmakers on Monday that Russia’s undeclared “shadow war” against Germany and its allies was escalating further and has “taken on a new, more dangerous character”. Berlin has invested record sums into rebuilding its military to deter Russia, and is among the largest supporters of Ukraine in the war with Moscow. In Brussels, EU foreign policy chief ⁠Kaja Kallas said Russia ⁠was putting lives at risk across Europe with hybrid attacks.
